commons:81707299.summary: On the ceiling of a burial chamber, Christ looks out frontally with long dark hair, a full beard and a halo, flanked by the Greek letters Alpha and Omega. Here the youthful shepherd of earlier catacomb art has given way to a mature, majestic figure, often cited as one of the earliest examples of the bearded type that would become the standard image of Christ. The letters proclaim him the beginning and the end, eternal Lord over life and death.
facts: The bearded, long-haired type draws on the dignified imagery of philosophers and of Jupiter, expressing Christ's authority and wisdom.

The painting is generally placed in the cubiculum of Leo, a burial chamber commissioned in the second half of the 4th century by Leo, an official of the annona (Rome's public grain supply), for himself and his family.
The catacomb, also called the Catacomb of Felix and Adauctus after the martyrs buried there, was rediscovered by Antonio Bosio in 1595, but the frescoed cubiculum of Leo came to light only in 1953.
Alpha and Omega, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, echo Christ's words in the Book of Revelation.
commons:81707299.notes: Dated 'late 4th century' by the Commons description; the exact chamber is not named there (it is often linked with the cubiculum of Leo, which could not be confirmed from the sources read). Image sourced from a secondary website, so check rights if a better photo is found.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-miraculous-draug.summary: The risen Christ stands on the shore beside a glowing charcoal fire, while the apostles, named in Latin labels (Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, Thomas), haul a net full of fish into their boat, and Peter wades ashore toward him. Beneath runs the text 'yet the disciples knew not that it was Jesus'.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.
Seven of its miniatures are attributed to the anonymous 'Master of the Registrum Gregorii', who worked in Trier.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-35-christ.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos sits in a globe-mandorla in the middle of the heavens with angels, above mountains cleft by a deep abyss where men sit and beasts graze. Beneath him an angel spreads his wings over 'the children of men' in a portico flanked by fountains from which birds spout water into men's cups, illustrating 'with thee is the fountain of life'. The psalmist stands below, gazing up.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-35-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects-freising-hodegetria-ivory.summary: The Virgin is shown in half-length holding the Christ Child on her left arm and pointing to him with her right hand, while two small busts of angels or saints appear in the upper corners. The Child, robed like an adult, sits upright and blesses. This is the Hodegetria ('She who shows the way'), in which Mary directs the viewer to her Son as the way to salvation.
facts: The Hodegetria type was named after a famous icon kept in the Hodegon monastery in Constantinople (tradition).
The Freising museum label describes the plaque as Byzantine, around 1000.

cur:objects-bm-baptism-of-christ-ivory.summary: John the Baptist, bearded and wearing a rough garment, lays his hand on the head of the young, naked Christ, who stands in the waters of the Jordan; the dove of the Holy Spirit descends from above, and angels attend with cloths. A small reclining figure at the bottom represents the river Jordan itself, a survival of classical personification. The panel shows the moment when Christ was revealed as the beloved Son.
facts: Early Christian images of the Baptism often show Christ as a small, youthful, naked figure and include a personification of the river Jordan, as here (type).

vam:O111098.summary: In crowded registers framed by a border of foliage, Christ hangs on the cross in a long tunic with a serpent at its foot, while Longinus pierces his side and Stephaton raises the sponge, the Virgin and St John standing near and the two thieves at the far edges. Below, an angel holding a cross sits on the open tomb and points the holy women to the Resurrection while soldiers sleep; elsewhere soldiers cast lots for Christ's garment and the Church drives out the Synagogue, and at the bottom Earth and Sea recline as witnesses. The ivory was recycled: the Carolingian carver worked on the back of the upper half of a 6th-century consular diptych leaf.
facts: The front of the plaque preserves the upper half of a consular diptych leaf of about 515–530, partly planed away; the lower half of the same leaf is in the British Museum, carved in the 9th century with the Betrayal and Mocking of Christ.
According to the V&A, this ivory and the British Museum Passion plaque together formed a book cover.
Elements of the composition, such as the personifications of Earth and Sea, follow the 'Liuthard group' ivories, notably the cover of the Pericopes of Henry II in Munich (about 860).
vam:O111098.notes: The worklist date (c. 515–530) belongs to the reused consular diptych, not to the Crucifixion carving, which the V&A dates to Metz, ca. 850–875. Formerly in the Webb collection.
